text: You now know how to find a matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Diagonalization is where that effort pays off: it repackages a matrix into a form where all its complexity gets pushed into two simple building blocks — a matrix of eigenvectors and a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

If an n by n matrix has n independent eigenvectors, you can build P, a matrix whose columns are those eigenvectors, and D, a diagonal matrix of the matching eigenvalues in the same order — and it's always true that A equals P D P inverse. Intuitively: P inverse converts into eigenvector coordinates, D does the easy part of scaling each one by its own eigenvalue, and P converts back.

For A equals 3,1,0,2, the eigenvalue 3 pairs with eigenvector 1,0, and the eigenvalue 2 pairs with eigenvector 1, negative 1. Building P from those eigenvectors as columns and D from the eigenvalues on the diagonal, and computing P inverse — which happens to equal P itself for this particular matrix.
Multiplying P times D gives 3,2,0, negative 2; multiplying that by P inverse reconstructs 3,1,0,2 — exactly the original matrix A. The factorization checks out.

One of diagonalization's biggest payoffs is computing high powers of a matrix cheaply: A to the k equals P, D to the k, P inverse, because every middle P inverse P pair cancels to the identity. And D to the k is trivial — just raise each diagonal entry to the k-th power. This exact pattern is why diagonalization matters when a quantum operation gets applied repeatedly.

Next lesson is the payoff for the whole chapter: when you measure a qubit, the only possible outcomes are the eigenvalues of what you're measuring, and the state collapses to the matching eigenvector.
